title: Waiting for Jay-Z
author: @NewYorker
content:
It was nearing midnight on a balmy Sunday in July, and there was still no sight of Jay-Z. This was the last of three sold-out concerts at Yankee Stadium, and somehow the tens of thousands of fans gathered inside didn’t appear too aggrieved, peaceably bopping along to old soul tunes on the P.A. and eating chicken tenders out of souvenir boxes shaped like Timberland boots. We take the magnitude of Jay for granted. “I made the Yankee hat more famous than a Yankee can,” he once rapped, a boast that’s come to seem less outlandish with time. No other artist has withstood hip-hop’s changing winds over such a long span, let alone won so many of the bets he placed on himself. Rap shows aren’t known for being tidy, punctual affairs anyway—what was another hour?

Then again, this was a crowd over-indexed in forty- and fiftysomethings, a demographic that would really feel the consequences of a late night come Monday morning. What drew so many people to these concerts, as well as to recent stadium shows in London and Paris this fall, was a sense of nostalgia and a perception of scarcity. Jay-Z’s previous solo tour was in 2017, after the release of “4:44,” an absorbing, stripped-down record full of post-therapy insights meant to repair his image after rumors of infidelity—transgressions that might have been bad enough even if his wife was not Beyoncé. The following year, the couple released “Everything Is Love,” a renewal of vows in album form, and toured Europe and North America as a double bill. In the near-decade since, Jay-Z has chosen his moments of visibility sparingly, appearing mostly as a power broker playing in one-per-center sandboxes. Although his gravitational effect on how people dress, what they sip at the club, and how they structure their bars has weakened, his presence is felt. “We tote guns to the Grammys, pop bottles on the White House lawn,” he rapped on “So Ghetto,” and it was a good, mischievous line back in 1999. But he has since become someone who texts Barack Obama, and who curates the most high-profile concert in the world, the Super Bowl halftime show.

The first night of the Yankee Stadium residency celebrated the thirtieth anniversary of Jay-Z’s début album, “Reasonable Doubt,” which he performed in its entirety, bringing out guests such as Beyoncé, Nas, and Alicia Keys. The following night, he did “The Blueprint,” from 2001, again with high-wattage support. Neither of these victory laps was preordained: hip-hop is a young person’s sport, and when “Reasonable Doubt” was released there was little reason to believe that Jay-Z, then twenty-six years old, would end up one of the greats. In the mid-nineties, the genre was dominated by prodigious, fully formed young talents such as Nas and the Notorious B.I.G. Jay had emerged a few years earlier, as the sidekick to a playfully spry Brooklyn rapper named Jaz-O, and had returned to selling drugs when both of their careers stalled. He eventually began to release his music through Roc-A-Fella, an independent record label that he’d started with some friends.

Jay-Z was early to realize that New York’s influence on hip-hop was waning, and that the lines dividing styles, regions, and genres were no longer as important as they once were. After “Reasonable Doubt,” a soulful, bruising masterpiece inspired by his native Brooklyn, he proved to be a shape-shifter and a shrewd collaborator, working with rappers from the South when this still seemed like a daring thing for an East Coast artist to do. In the five years between “Reasonable Doubt” and “The Blueprint”—which was released on September 11, 2001—he went from being yet another New York rapper scrapping for relevance to being hip-hop’s undisputed king. And then he somehow kept ascending, sanding down the edges of his persona until he became the quintessential celebrity of the Obama era, back when the notion of doing unprecedented things and entering off-limits rooms felt transgressive enough. He invested in restaurants, created beverage and clothing lines, and became a part owner of the New Jersey Nets, helping oversee the team’s relocation to Brooklyn. In 2005, he rapped, prophetically, “I’m not a businessman, I’m a business, man.”

This last concert of the Yankee Stadium run promised to be a career-spanning revue—an enticing pitch, as the later albums have felt more like exercises in brand management. “Magna Carta Holy Grail,” released in 2013, was initially a free download exclusively for Samsung customers; “4:44” seemed partly an attempt to boost subscriptions to Tidal, a streaming company that he owned. Maybe, for Jay-Z, these were the only victories worth pursuing anymore. Perhaps after years of fending off challenges from rival New York rappers, there was a novelty to hanging out with Bono and Chris Martin—or Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner—instead. This was as plausible an explanation for the delay as any: a guest on the level of a world leader. With Jay, anything seems possible.

When Jay-Z first announced his return to the stage, he sat for an extended interview with GQ, complete with a photo shoot by the artist Rashid Johnson, whose work he collects. His comments illustrated the unique burden of the hip-hop superstar, straining to stay in touch with the grimy realism of his earliest rhymes. He wondered aloud if rap’s hypercompetitive battle culture, as recently embodied by Kendrick Lamar and Drake, had become too much of a liability. (“I don’t know if it’s worth it at this point.”) He called the rising tide of anti-billionaire sentiment in America a “cop-out,” sounding slightly defensive. His wealth hasn’t changed his sense of morality, he explained. “A person with more money can do more good. . . . This is the system that we have. And with the system that we have, what are you going to do?” The elephant in the room was a lawsuit, filed in 2024 and withdrawn in 2025, in which an anonymous woman had accused him and Diddy of sexually assaulting her when she was a teen-ager. “That shit took a lot out of me,” he said. “I was angry. I haven’t been that angry in a long time.”

Jay-Z opened the first night at Yankee Stadium with a kind of State of the Union freestyle. He hinted that Colin Kaepernick, the former N.F.L. quarterback, whom many believe to have been blackballed by the league for his advocacy against police brutality, wasn’t as righteous as we thought. Jay argued that he had chosen a less showy way to make change, advocating for criminal-justice reform out of the spotlight. “I’m the one they can’t control,” he rapped, suggesting that Kaepernick had taken an unreported payout from the N.F.L. and dismissing the “Twitter activists” who didn’t see the long game of his backroom advocacy.

The backroom becomes literal in “Jaÿ-Z in 8,” a new eight-part documentary series on HBO featuring the rapper in conversation with the producer Rick Rubin, who has been anointed a mascot of sorts for the notion of creativity. Each episode shows the two men sitting in the Palais Brongniart, in Paris, listening to Jay’s songs on a very nice sound system, and talking about them. “This is like elder wisdom,” Rubin says excitedly, after playing “Don’t You Know,” a preternaturally mature track from 2002. “It’s really wild,” Jay agrees. “I don’t know where it was coming from.”

Their conversations drift from Jay’s memories of his late, long-estranged father to his experience with therapy, measuring the distance between the brash playboy of then and the fifty-six-year-old family man of now. The series ends up being the latest retelling of a story that fans know well at this point—I still prefer “Fade to Black,” from 2004, a behind-the-scenes film about the making of “The Black Album,” and “Decoded,” from 2010, an autobiography co-authored with the journalist dream hampton. What distinguishes this new project is Jay’s obvious delight in having Rubin, the eccentric naïf, as his interlocutor and audience. (Rubin played the same role for Paul McCartney in “McCartney 3,2,1,” a six-part documentary from 2021.) “You knew so much,” Rubin effuses about the early music. “It’s amazing.”

The pair’s narration of Jay-Z’s life doubles as a history of America in the past half century, beginning with the economic collapse of New York in the seventies, running through the rise of rap, the crack epidemic, and the war on drugs, and landing on the eventual pathbreaking successes of the hip-hop generation. Jay has always skillfully folded each turn into his larger mythology, going from drug dealer to rapper to label boss to executive with an air of inevitability, every choice subsumed into the glory of the hustle. “Have you been the same person the whole time?” Rubin asks innocently. No, Jay replies. He was constantly becoming someone different.

It was Monday by the time Jay-Z took the stage. As the introduction to “The Dynasty: Roc La Familia” pulsed through the Stadium, he stepped out wearing a Yankees cap and a bespoke pin-striped workwear suit, looking like the most elegant handyman on Earth. His band turned the song into a headbanger’s delight; Jay remained steady and regal over the crunching guitar chords and cathartic drum kicks. When it was over, he took a moment to explain the delay. Some fans had breached one of the entrances without paying, leading security to shut down the entire Stadium. Jay had insisted on waiting until every ticket holder was allowed in before performing. But he promised that he would not be shortchanging us.

Jay was limber and cocky, unhurried as he prowled the stage. We had been waiting for four hours, desperate for a release, yet he was assured and deliberate with every move. His strength in the late nineties was a kind of calm under pressure, and his power in the next decade was translating that swaggering cool for ever-larger stages. Songs that felt tense and claustrophobic on the records—such as “Where I’m From,” a track from 1997 about the Marcy Projects—became seismic events when performed live.

At one point, Jay removed his jacket and revealed what appeared to be a bulletproof vest—a nod to the “Streets Is Watching” video, from 1998, when his paranoia toward his rivals was at its highest. The delirium of the late hour only deepened as the guests came out: Jeezy, Teyana Taylor, Jermaine Dupri, Usher, Swizz Beatz, Rihanna (who briefly out-swaggered Jay), Pharrell, and Beyoncé, backed by the Mayyas, a Lebanese dance group. These were all stars he could either claim credit for making or consider of equal stature. Even more impressive was how they had all stayed hours past their presumed call times. I felt silly for thinking that the evening’s guests might have been fellow nineties stalwarts such as M.O.P. or Cam’ron. The legacy that Jay wanted to broadcast was not one in which he acknowledged his generational peers, many of whom are more likely to feature on back-in-the-day podcasts than on new tracks.

For a couple of hours, it was easy to forget who Jay had become, and to instead marvel that he was still here at all. So many of the supporting characters of his rise were absent, whether they had lost their place in his inner circle, such as his Roc-A-Fella co-founder Damon Dash, or died before their time, as with the Notorious B.I.G. and DMX. Of course, there was no Diddy or R. Kelly, both incarcerated for sexual misconduct. The most auspicious absence was Kanye West, Jay’s estranged former protégé, who is arguably the only other solo rapper who could draw crowds of this size.

An elevated subway train rumbled by in the distance, just past the outfield, a reminder of the city beyond. How could Jay-Z possibly stay connected to the world that his music was designed to escape? Standing in the audience, I thought about hearing “Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem)” for the first time, recognizing that it was sampling the musical “Annie,” and finding this both absurd and totally irresistible. I remembered how effortlessly Jay took to hip-hop’s evolutionary turns in the late nineties and early two-thousands, moving from New York’s stoic classicism to the squeak and space-age funk of producers like Timbaland and the Neptunes. I thought about the hours I’d spent in the d.j. booth trying to figure out how to mix in and out of “Big Pimpin’ ” or admiring the blunt simplicity of “Money, Cash, Hoes,” which still sounds to me like someone getting frustrated with a keyboard and throwing it down a stairwell.

I looked around and imagined everyone was similarly adrift, all of us in our own orbits, with Jay the common gravitational center. Yankee Stadium felt small and intimate. My friend and I left during the encore, as he began “Empire State of Mind,” a song that became so ubiquitous during the Knicks playoff run this spring that I never need to hear it again. It seemed more sensible to beat the traffic. ♦

title: “Resident Evil” Is Fun, but Soulless. What Else Could It Be?
author: @NewYorker
content:
It would be hard to overstate the influence of Resident Evil. The franchise, one of the most successful ever, spans thirty-odd games—many of which are very good—and has spawned multiple live-action film adaptations and television shows, nearly all of which have been terrible. The games, which follow the survivors of a zombie outbreak induced by a corporate bioweapon, popularized a genre known as survival horror, in which a normie character—as opposed to the typical overpowered hero—must carefully navigate a dangerous environment, conserving ammo and other resources, solving puzzles, and evading enemies almost as often as fighting them. (One can imagine how this would appeal to a certain kind of personality.) These games, alongside their first film adaptation, in 2002, helped revive the zombie-film genre, which had peaked in 1978 with George Romero’s “Dawn of the Dead,” before dying out in the late nineteen-eighties, as audiences moved on to smarter monsters: vampires, serial killers, Chucky.

Today, the Resident Evil franchise holds the record for the most live-action films based on a video-game series. The movies occupy a strange cultural position, though, making up a commercially successful franchise with basically zero critical acclaim. Salon described the first installment as “mildly grisly, assaultively noisy and tremendously boring”; Roger Ebert put the film and its sequel, “Resident Evil: Apocalypse,” on his most-hated-films list. The movies have been most controversial among fans of the games because of their distance from the original source material. (It certainly didn’t help that the writer and director, Paul W. S. Anderson, created a new protagonist for his films, an ass-kicking yet spiritually empty heroine named Alice—played by Milla Jovovich, his wife.) Hollywood has long puzzled over the problem of video-game adaptations: change the plot too much and alienate the fans; hew too closely to the game and alienate the masses. Either way, these adaptations—even the well-respected ones, such as “The Last of Us,” on HBO, or “Fallout,” on Prime Video—necessarily lack the thing that makes a video game enjoyable: the experience of playing it.

This is why Zach Cregger’s new “Resident Evil” movie, which premièred last week, is an undeniable feat. The film is a loving homage to the sensation of playing a survival-horror game. We shift environments every few minutes, with the set pieces becoming increasingly elaborate, and the enemies increasingly deadly—mirroring the experience of moving from one level to the next. The movie opens on a young, schlubby guy named Bryan, brilliantly embodied by the actor Austin Abrams, who played a drug addict in Cregger’s previous film, “Weapons.” Bryan has a very wholesome job: delivering organs to hospitals where they’ll be used for transplants. And yet we can also tell, as he shuffles haplessly through a crowded hospital, looking like an extra in his own life, that he is not a great guy, but a disappointingly ordinary one. He is what’s known in the video-game world as an N.P.C., or a non-player character. Here, though, he’s also our hero, which means that after he’s commissioned to deliver a crucial package to another hospital—he thinks that it’s an organ, but he later discovers that it’s something scientists need in order to make an antidote for the virus they’ve accidentally unleashed—we get to watch him struggle his way through a monster-ridden wasteland that he has no business being in. Among the zombies he encounters, the mutations range: one creature’s face splits open like a flower, revealing an enormous eye and far too many teeth; another is a morbidly obese sewer dweller. More frequently than not, tentacles are involved. It’s solid body horror, but the film’s minor touches are what make it shine as an adaptation. While exploring a seemingly deserted farmhouse, Bryan finds a shotgun in one room, then must search the rest of the house for the shells, an experience familiar to anyone who’s ever played a Resident Evil game. He constantly fires at padlocks trying to open them, not realizing that he’s going to need to find a key somewhere.

Cregger’s film is on track to become the most profitable movie in the entire “Resident Evil” series, grossing sixty million dollars domestically in its opening weekend. GQ and Esquire have declared it the best video-game adaptation ever, and it probably is. But, in the context of Cregger’s œuvre, this thrilling, well-crafted film still feels slightly disappointing, which is less a knock on the movie than it is a recognition of how we engage with auteurs.

I went to see “Resident Evil” because I’m a Zach Cregger fan, and I enjoyed it less than I otherwise would have because I’m a Zach Cregger fan. The director is one of the most exciting filmmakers today, known for his structurally and tonally audacious—and also genuinely fear-inducing and hilarious—movies. He is operating at a level matched only by Jordan Peele and Ari Aster. His 2022 film, “Barbarian,” has one the cleverest setups of any horror movie I’ve seen: A woman arrives at a house rental in the middle of the night only to discover that a strange man is already staying there. They must have been double-booked; does she want to come inside so they can figure out what to do? Cregger had said that he was inspired by “The Gift of Fear,” a 1997 self-help guide by the security expert Gavin de Becker, which encourages women to trust their subconscious and to pay attention to subtle red flags in their interactions with men. (The movie began as a creative exercise, in which Cregger set out to write a scene that included as many of these red flags as possible—ones that women would notice but men would miss.) As the movie continues, we switch between different characters’ perspectives, and move back and forth in time. The film is uneven, but also relentlessly innovative.

“Weapons,” released in 2025, was both much more ambitious and far more disciplined. It follows a suburban town in the aftermath of a tragedy: seventeen children, all from the same class, vanish from their homes on the same night, sparking a community-wide witch hunt initially aimed at the children’s teacher. (The real witch responsible, played by Amy Madigan, won an Oscar for her performance.) “Weapons” has been widely interpreted as an allegory for mass shootings. There’s the title, of course, and then the concept of an entire classroom disappearing at once. The seventeen children—the same number of kids and adults who were murdered in the Parkland shooting—disappear at 2:17 A.M., which viewers speculated might be a reference to the number of members of the House of Representatives who voted, in 2022, for a ban on assault weapons that never became law. At one point, a grieving father, played by Josh Brolin, dreams of an assault weapon floating over a neighbor’s house: an AR imprinted with 2:17. Cregger has denied that the movie is about shootings, saying that he was mostly interested in exploring how alcoholism can destroy a family. But what about the dream? “I don’t know,” Cregger said, when an interviewer asked him what it meant. “It’s a very important moment for me in this movie, and to be frank with you, I think what I love about it so much is that I don’t understand it.”

I believe that “Weapons” is about guns, regardless of whether that was Cregger’s initial intention. But I don’t blame him for not actively embracing that interpretation, seeing how it might get in the way of, say, rebooting a video-game franchise with guns. One of the running gags in “Resident Evil” is Bryan’s ineptitude with firearms. “I’ve only used guns in video games. It’s confusing in real life,” he says, before accidentally firing off an MP-5 submachine gun inside a car. Just as a player grows in proficiency as she makes her way through a game, Bryan’s narrative arc largely consists of him becoming a more competent marksman.

In one of the film’s most memorable scenes, Bryan, newly armed with a shotgun, ventures into an R.V., where he encounters a young girl. She’s beginning to mutate; one of her legs has sprouted tentacles. He tries to save her, but she turns hostile, at which point, he blows her head off. The scene offers a double shock: it’s rare to see a child killed in a horror movie (notably, in “Weapons,” none of the children died), and it’s rarer yet for a child to be killed by the protagonist. Even Bryan doesn’t believe it. “I didn’t just shoot a little girl in the face,” he tells himself. “I like kids.” The sequence is one of the more disturbing—and, yes, funny—set pieces in the movie, and it felt deliberate, as if Cregger were taking aim, so to speak, at the discourse around his previous work. I didn’t read the scene as a disavowal so much as a pointed reminder that “Resident Evil,” unlike “Barbarian” and “Weapons,” isn’t that interested in mining the psychological depths of its characters. What Cregger has created here is a ninety-five-minute romp, a reboot that’s meant to be considered alongside a different canon than his own.

The main thing we know about Bryan, aside from the fact that he’s a “glorified Postmates driver,” in his words, is that his girlfriend is pregnant; the film begins with him learning this over the phone, and failing to meet the moment. In what’s meant to be “Resident Evil” ’s emotional climax, Bryan, increasingly worried that he’s not going to make it back home, sits in a parking garage and records a voice memo for her: “I hate that my first reaction was just me being afraid of change or growing up,” he says. Yet, almost as soon as Bryan begins to cry, he’s interrupted by a scientist addressing him through the parking-garage intercom: “Yeah, you, crying guy.” It’s the voice of Cregger himself, who, in an audio-only cameo, gives Bryan directions to a lab, on the twenty-eighth floor of the building, where scientists are working on the cure to the unleashed virus.

I later realized that the voice-memo scene captures, rather shrewdly, a common feature of video games, in which players stumble upon recordings from the poor N.P.C.s who died making the same journey before them. But, as a stand-alone scene, Bryan’s tearful goodbye message feels rote—which perhaps Cregger knows, hence why he quickly interjects so that we can return to the action. Another movie, an emotionally rich one, the kind that we know Cregger can make, would have lingered on the moment. Bryan is an N.P.C., though, and so maybe Cregger is doing us a favor by preventing us from getting too attached. The true emotional climax of “Resident Evil” comes several minutes later, when Bryan, staring down two enemy threats at once, takes a deep breath, aims his handgun—which has a single bullet left—and finally gets off a good shot. “Yeah!” he shouts. “Video games!” ♦

title: The Worlds That Donald Trump and Xi Jinping Want
author: @NewYorker
content:
When the plane bearing the Chinese President, Xi Jinping, lands at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday afternoon, his American counterpart will be waiting for him. U.S. Presidents usually receive heads of state at the White House, but the esteem with which Donald Trump appears to hold Xi, and the weight of this visit from the leader of the United States’ closest peer competitor—the first of its kind in a decade—are apparently such that Trump decided to greet him on the tarmac. On Thursday, when Xi goes to the White House, the two leaders will hear the U.S. Marine Band play both of their national anthems and watch a military flyover featuring a B-2 stealth bomber and four F-22 Raptors. When the President went to Beijing in May, he did not get an airport pickup from Xi, and when Xi later escorted him to the Great Hall of the People, they were met by a group of children, who chanted “Welcome!” and waved Chinese and American flags. Optics are paramount for Xi, who presides over a sprawling but opaque one-party state apparatus, and comes to the United States leaving behind a mounting set of domestic woes, including sluggish economic growth and stubbornly high youth unemployment. But he will begin his time in Washington as Trump’s honored guest, more fêted than leaders of allied nations who have called on Trump during his turbulent second term.

What will follow—closed-door meetings between Trump and Xi, with their staffers, scheduled amid the hurried summitry; a state dinner crowded with tech C.E.O.s and other A-listers; a tea involving the Presidents and their spouses, all of it likely covered by a reduced press corps following Trump’s ban on three major media outlets—is murkier. Despite the pomp, expectations for tangible results are low, with Trump and Xi’s personal rapport belying a chasm of distrust and tension between Beijing and Washington.

China has played a central role in the past decade of Trumpist politics. Initially, for Trump the campaigner, China was the embodiment of U.S. folly, a country catapulted to superpower status thanks to the naïveté and the cupidity of the American globalist class, which, a generation ago, opened the doors for China’s manufacturing juggernaut to take over the global economy, hollowing out factories and disappearing working-class jobs in the West. For Trump the President, China was, in his first term, a clear strategic rival to be reined in by tough policies, including the first blows of a trade war that lingered through the Biden Administration, which took a similarly tough, if more calibrated, approach to Beijing. But, in Trump’s second term, his tone has changed—in April of last year, China responded to his unprecedented tariffs with expanded export controls that showcased the dominance of its critical-mineral supply chains, which many U.S. companies depend on. Trump backtracked, and has conspicuously softened his stance. He delayed arms sales to Taiwan, the autonomous island democracy whose return to mainland rule Xi says is a “historical inevitability,” and appears to have tolerated China’s insufficient purchases of U.S. agricultural products that Xi had pledged to fulfill.

Potential positive outcomes from the summit may include the start of a formal U.S.-China dialogue over A.I. and its perils, and an agreement to extend a trade truce reached last October, which saw the Trump Administration scale back some of its tariffs on Chinese goods, and saw China maintain certain exports of critical minerals. (Many Western, Indian, and Japanese manufacturers complain of ongoing difficulties in sourcing these elements.) Friction certainly remains between the two nations—from the Pacific, where U.S. preëminence is constantly being eroded by China’s rise, to wars in the Middle East and Europe, where China is tacitly backing U.S. adversaries—but, lately, Trump prefers to spotlight his admiration for the Chinese President. “He’s a great gentleman. We get along great,” Trump said earlier this month. “We have a very good trading relationship, and, you know, they’re a competitor and all of that, but we have a very good relationship with President Xi.”

Whether Xi is moved by Trump’s bonhomie may be immaterial. Analysts see China working quietly in the shadow of Trump’s blustering disruption. In some sectors, it is gingerly filling the void left by Trump’s America First agenda, including buttressing parts of the global humanitarian system gutted by the Administration’s dismantling of U.S.A.I.D. More broadly, China is gaining ground simply by existing in contrast to Trump’s United States—a more predictable power that’s not launching unprovoked wars, installing puppet regimes in petro-states, or erratically lashing out at longtime friends and partners. (New polling confirms the impression of China’s growing popularity around the world, relative to the United States.) On Tuesday, at the dais of the U.N.’s General Assembly, Trump denounced the institution’s “globalist bureaucrats who nobody ever elected” and its “far-left” agendas, attacking bodies such as its human-rights council, and the International Criminal Court. He laid out possible strikes against Iran, musing, “Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” (The King of Jordan, speaking right after Trump, bemoaned the global instability wrought by the Iran war.) Trump also celebrated his military operation, earlier this year, in Venezuela, to remove Nicolás Maduro from power, asserting that the U.S. “will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States.” Here was the leader of the global hegemon, reminding the world of his hegemony.

Other world leaders at the General Assembly, including Brazil’s President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who immediately preceded Trump, took turns offering an alternate world view, extolling the virtues of “multilateralism” and invoking the need for greater coöperation and the bolstering of U.N. institutions. “Sovereignty is strengthened, not diminished, when countries work together to address shared challenges,” Lula, together with Prime Minister Mark Carney, of Canada; President William Ruto, of Kenya; and António Costa, the president of the European Council, said in an opinion piece for the Financial Times on Sunday. They added, “National interests are often best advanced through collective action on such challenges.” That’s an ethos wholly rejected by Trump, of course, but one that suits China, at least as rhetoric. Xi comes to Washington following a tour through Central Asia and South Asia, where he cast China as a driver of a revived global order that engages in multilateralism and offered his now routine critique of great power “hegemonism” —a barely veiled jab at Trump. Beijing, in standard Communist Party jargon, says that it wants to address “global governance deficits,” and for China to be a “responsible major country” that can champion the causes of nations in the so-called Global South which have been underrepresented in the post-1945 international system and hurt by decades of unfair and domineering Western economic practices.

In fact, governments in the developing world have concerns about Beijing’s designs and practices, but they can’t ignore China’s economic footprint—it is most countries’ biggest trading partner—and they are all, in various ways, trying to hedge against an increasingly unreliable Washington. At a forum in Beijing last week, Singapore’s defense minister, Chan Chun Sing, whose city-state lies at the heart of major global trade, lamented how some powers have “tried to weaponize their economic interdependence”—an implicit criticism of Trump’s tariffs, but also, perhaps, of how China often leverages its significant industrial and supply-chain advantages.

In curious ways, Trump and Xi mirror each other. They “both regard themselves as seminal, if not singular, figures whom history has appointed to fulfill a weighty mandate,” Ali Wyne, a researcher at the International Crisis Group, told me. That is, he said, they see themselves as “insuring that their respective countries regain the greatness squandered by predecessors” because of “corruption, ineptness, and timidity.” Trump has gone about pursuing this reclamation by smashing the trust of close U.S. allies with coercive, bullying tactics. “Historically, Washington saw its alliances as the starting point for international diplomacy,” Rush Doshi, a China scholar at Georgetown University and the Council on Foreign Relations, and a veteran of the Biden White House, told me. “Trump often flips the script, seeing the other great powers—particularly Beijing and Moscow—as the starting point.” That view “suits Beijing well,” Doshi added, since China is averse to treaty alliances, but is eager for the kind of great-power shoulder-rubbing that will be on show this week in Washington. “Trump’s approach, in many ways, is what they have long had in mind,” he said.

What does Xi now seem to have in mind? Kevin Rudd, a former Prime Minister of Australia and a noted China expert, points to the centrality of Xi’s never-ending campaign to consolidate and extend his own power, buttressed by his staunch Marxist-Leninist bona fides and his ruthless focus on preserving and controlling the ruling Communist Party, whose cadres he has frequently purged. Jessica Chen Weiss, a former State Department official and a professor at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, argued on a recent podcast that China favors “a small-C conservative” norms in the international system, in which non-interference in the affairs of other sovereign states is paramount, suggesting that China’s expansive nationalist project parallels an America First agenda. Ryan Hass, a China expert at the Brookings Institution who served in the Obama White House, recently wrote that Beijing “views America as declining but dangerous,” and that Xi is “content to patiently accumulate power and influence until such time as the country becomes broadly recognized as leader of a new political order.”

In Trump, Beijing could have an unwitting accomplice. Evan Feigenbaum, a Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Asia during the George W. Bush Administration, argued that China has found an “easy mark,” who is giving ground on sensitive issues such as export controls on U.S. chips and American policy toward Taiwan. Still, China is not aiming for a grand bargain with Washington anytime soon. “Their objective really is just to ring-fence the worst outcomes and park the Americans in a corner,” Feigenbaum told me, “and then pursue their opportunities for expansion of their influence regionally and globally elsewhere.” ♦

title: What Life Is Actually Like in Gaza Today
author: @NewYorker
content:
At least twenty-one people, many of them children, were killed earlier this week after a building collapsed in Gaza City, highlighting the dangerous conditions that still exist in the Gaza Strip. The building, like much of the remaining infrastructure in Gaza, had been damaged by Israeli strikes in the war that began after the massacre of October 7, 2023, and which has now killed seventy-four thousand Palestinians. More than thirteen hundred of those deaths have occurred since last October, when a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas went into effect, and Israel was left in control of just over half of Gaza. (Since the ceasefire, Israel has expanded its territory and now controls around seventy per cent of the strip.) The Trump Administration, which broadly supports Israeli policy, has given authority to the so-called Board of Peace to oversee Gaza’s reconstruction. But last month the board’s high representative for Gaza took the surprising step of criticizing Israel for its continued military strikes in Gaza, and argued that such attacks threaten both the ceasefire and the chances of Hamas ever disarming.

I recently spoke by phone with Jaser AbuMousa, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, and a non-resident policy adviser at the International Peace Institute, who was born and raised in Gaza. During our conversation, which has been edited for length and clarity, we discussed what daily life in Gaza is like for Palestinians, what has and has not changed since the ceasefire, and his own family’s horrific experience throughout the past three years.

To what degree have Gazans been able to establish somewhat of a normal life over the past eleven months, since the ceasefire went into effect? How much have Gazans been able to start to rebuild their lives, and how much are they essentially still living in a war zone?

What we know is that, because Israel controls about seventy per cent of the territory of the Gaza Strip, some two million people are squeezed into thirty per cent of the territory. We know that eighty-one per cent of the Gaza Strip is damaged or destroyed, and more than three hundred thousand housing units were completely destroyed during the war, in addition to schools and other infrastructure, like clinics, hospitals, and mosques. But, after the ceasefire, and especially in January of 2026, when Israel recovered the last hostage’s remains, many people in Gaza were happy and thought that they would be able to start to restore their lives.

However, this did not happen. And then there was the Israeli condition that Hamas disarmament should come first, and then the rest of the promises outlined in the ceasefire could follow. If I were in Gaza right now, there is a fifty-per-cent chance that I would be living in a tent or living in the remains of my house. Many people prefer to live in the ruins of their houses instead of having tents because the tents do not protect them from any kind of rain or any kind of heat, and there are also rodents that spread diseases.

On the other side of things, some people have started to show some signs of civic engagement. They have started to reopen restaurants. There have been more weddings. But all of this did not cancel the fact that there is no construction material entering Gaza. There is no construction equipment to clear the rubble in Gaza. There are still a lot of constraints, even on food items like peanut butter. I was surprised to hear this directly from U.N. personnel, about peanut butter not being allowed into Gaza. So the people are striving to restore some sort of normal life, but they cannot do this because, first of all, hundreds of thousands of children are not going to school for the third year in a row, and the universities are destroyed, and there is unprecedented internal violence among the people in Gaza. I saw how people inflicted violence on each other during the war in 2014. And the magnitude of this war is much greater than in 2014, so it’s very much expected.

When you say you saw people in Gaza inflict violence on themselves, do you mean that there’s intra-Gaza conflict just because of how horrible the war has been?

Yes. For example, a couple of days ago, three people were killed in a water queue. They were filling water from a truck, and suddenly there was a problem and they killed each other. Every day, cases like this are registered. And, unfortunately, in addition to domestic violence, in addition to violence against vulnerable groups like women and children, this sort of thing is widespread. And, unfortunately, this is not going to change soon. I mean, we have a very damaged society in the Gaza Strip right now owing to the magnitude of violence and the restrictions that are imposed on people. And we have, let’s say, malbehavior. There is a phrase that has stuck with me: that the people of Gaza developed “lethal survival skills,” especially during the starvation that happened last year.

I read about the peanut butter. Aid workers and Palestinians are hoping to get peanut butter because it functions as a nutritional supplement for people who have not gotten enough nutrition, and it sounds insane, but the Israeli government is claiming that it is a“luxury.”

It is insane, because, on the other hand, they are allowing chocolates and they are allowing sugar into Gaza, but they do not allow something like peanut butter, which is nutritious. The U.N. was hoping that it would be helpful because of all the malnutrition that the people are suffering from. So their claim that it’s a luxury is nonsense.

When you said that eighty-one per cent of Gaza is unlivable, what did you mean?

Yes, eighty-one per cent of infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed, according to U.N. statistics. One related issue we have is a very, very severe problem with sewage. There is no single sewage network that is still working. The only places it is working partially are places where everything was not destroyed.

What are the areas in Gaza that Israel has taken over since the ceasefire was put in place?

This has different layers. First of all, if we look at the map, it has the initial lines of the ceasefire, called the “Yellow Line” and demarcated by yellow cement blocks, which established that fifty-three per cent of Gaza would be under Israeli control and forty-seven per cent would be under Hamas control. After the ceasefire, Israel started to move to the west, and they started to move the yellow cement blocks. This created agricultural problems because the areas that Israel took control of after the ceasefire were the food basket of the Gaza Strip. And now the agricultural production level is, like, three per cent to five per cent of the level that it was before. So in some areas, Gaza was once self-sufficient, in terms of producing olive oil, olives, zucchini, eggplants, cucumbers, and peppers, and of course tomatoes. And at some points in recent years they were exporting tomatoes to Israel. So all of this is gone, and Gazans are not able to produce any kind of food for themselves. So they have to import it, and then that has to be under Israeli control.

I’m sure you’re still in touch with people in Gaza. What is the tone of those conversations now, and how do they differ from how they were during the war and how they were earlier on in the ceasefire?

Do you know what happened with me, or not?

I know that your wife and two of your kids were killed early on in the war.

Yeah. And later on, in July, 2025, my mother and my sister and her children were also killed. And when they were seeking refuge at my uncle’s house, he was killed, too, with his wife.

I’m sorry to hear that.

Thank you. So I’m still in contact with people. My brother was in prison for twenty months. He was a doctor in a hospital. He also lost his son. He was taken from Nasser Hospital when the Israeli troops stormed the hospital in February, 2024, and he was released on the day of the ceasefire. But of course I still have family. I still have friends. The tone is completely desperate, to be honest. I mean, the waiting without anything moving is making people angry, and they cannot respond positively. I mean, they cannot engage in a normal conversation. I understand this. I totally understand this.

I will give you an example of this. In July, 2025, two days or two nights before my mother was killed, I called her. My mother was seventy-five years old. She had a car accident years ago, and she was suffering from bad legs and her right arm was totally paralyzed, and I told her that the Israeli tanks were around her area and she needed to move. She said, “No, I’m not moving. Whatever happens, happens. I will not move this time.” My mother was displaced six times with this health condition, and, eventually, she was desperate. She was saying, “No, not anymore.” And she chose to die, apparently. This kind of atmosphere is prevailing in Gaza, and everyone that I’m talking to in Gaza is wishing to get out of Gaza. Everyone—literally everyone. And people are paying a lot of money to get access to bad medical reports so they can be evacuated medically or be accepted for a scholarship or something. I mean, three years. It’s been three years right now with life totally on hold.

When your mother said that to you, what did you say to her, if you don't mind me asking?

I was speechless, and I did not argue with her because, two weeks before that call, I think it was the second Eid of Muslims, and I knew, even though she did not tell me, that she had spent that night in the street, because they were forced to leave the area she was in at night. And I could not argue. I mean, I was not in her shoes. I left Gaza after two months. I was not displaced. I did not experience any kind of starvation. But my mother had. My mother had been displaced and had been starved, and I cannot blame anyone in these conditions, whatever their decision is. Yeah.

Why was your brother in prison?

He was just taken from the hospital, and he was tried four times before a military judge, and every time he was told that they didn’t have anything on him. But they also said, “You will not be released before the ceasefire.” And this message was given to many other medical staff, actually, because they wanted to deliberately deprive the medical institutions of staff. [While Israel has denied intentionally attacking Gaza’s health-care system, human-rights organizations and the United Nations have found that Gaza’s health system has been targeted.] He was taken because he was a doctor. And they kept him in prison without any charges.

And you can look at Hussam Abu Safiya’s case. He is another doctor who has been held without charges.

I just have one more question for you, and if it’s too personal, please—

Sure.

You have obviously been through just horrific tragedy, and you’re also someone who works on this subject. You think about this subject most of the day, I imagine, and not just the interpersonal dynamics but the geopolitics and the larger questions involved. And I’m just curious what that’s been like for you to continue writing and doing work on this subject while at the same time going through such awful horror. Is it therapeutic? Is it helpful?

First of all, it is therapeutic, and I appreciate everyone who has encouraged me to write. And the first one was my wife, Heba, many long years ago. She said, “You can be a good writer.” I did not believe her because she was a poet and she was a novelist, and, when I compared myself to her, it was a vast difference. But, I mean, she’s the one who encouraged me a long time ago to write. This is one. Second, I try to write things that seek a solution. I’m working with the Middle East Institute. I’m also working with the International Peace Institute, and we are trying to promote some solutions. We are also working with the group A Land for All, which is made up of Israelis and Palestinians. We also work with the group Standing Together. And I also do speaking engagements with an Israeli co-host. We have a podcast as well. So we are promoting something that we hope lasts. We want this to end. The people want it to end and to stop burying their children.

I’m also doing this for my kids. I want to give them some sort of normality and some sort of mutuality, and so I am telling them that what happened on the seventh of October and after was not normal. It is the exception. So this is what I’m trying to do. I’m partnering with an Israeli American writer in Boston. She and I are translating my wife’s work into English. So my wife has, or had, a poetry collection, and we had a reading in Cambridge in June, and the place was fully packed with people.

It is wonderful to hear that. How many kids did you have?

I had four. I lost the eldest and the youngest.

How old were they?

Hmaid was eighteen, and Abdulrahman was eight.

And you’re with your two middle kids now?

Yeah, Abdallah, now nineteen, and Sham, now fifteen, are with me. We came in January, 2025, and Sham did not speak English when we came here. And in June she graduated from middle school, and she was chosen to deliver the promotional speech at the school’s ceremony. I think that was a moment. That was a very, very good moment. ♦

title: The Trump Administration Is Trying to Get Musk and X Out of a $137 Million EU Fine
author: @wired
content:
The US government is trying to get Elon Musk and his social media platform X out of a $137 million fine by the European Union in an escalation of its criticism of the bloc’s tech rules.

The US Department of Justice said it had filed an application with the help of the Department of State to support a legal challenge by Musk to annul the case in the EU’s General Court. The Luxembourg-based court will now decide whether the US has a right to intervene.

The US government is arguing that it should be involved in the case to protect American companies. The fine is precedent-setting as the bloc’s first sanction under the Digital Services Act, which requires online platforms to do more to tackle illegal and harmful content, especially the largest sites. Many of those, which include Meta’s Facebook and Instagram, Google’s YouTube, and Microsoft’s LinkedIn, are headquartered in the US and contribute significantly to the US economy, it pointed out.

“We will not tolerate the European Commission engaging in regulatory overreach to try and control American engines of innovation and economic growth,” said assistant attorney general Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division.

The case also has “implications” for US-EU relations, it warned. The act has become a major source of tension between officials, with US President Donald Trump calling the penalties “overseas extortion.” Last year, he threatened imposing tariffs on any country implementing digital regulation, which he said were “all designed to harm, or discriminate against, American technology.” Vice President JD Vance has criticized the DS’s content moderation rules as “authoritarian censorship.”

The European Commission slapped X with the €120 million fine in December following a two-year-long investigation which found X had breached transparency obligations. Claiming users with blue checkmarks are “verified accounts” when they simply have to pay for the status is deceptive, the Commission ruled. X’s inaccessible and incomplete advertising repository and failure to provide access to public data for researchers is also hindering research into the platform’s risks, it said. In July, the Commission accepted X’s plan to fix the data access issues, which X now has six months to implement.

Both Musk and X launched appeals against the ruling on behalf of both parties in February. The EU’s investigation was “incomplete and superficial” and the interpretation of the DSA obligations “tortured,” they said. They also complained they had not been given “rights of defence … suggesting prosecutorial bias.”

Musk has also complained about the financial and administrative burden of heightened transparency requirements as governments globally try to get a better understanding of—and limit—social media platforms’ risks of harm. In July, he argued Australia’s “invasive” information-gathering powers within the country’s under-16 social media ban interfered with international law. At the time, professor of internet law at Queen Mary University of London, Julia Hörnle, told WIRED that Australian regulators were within their rights to order disclosures related to a company’s operations in that particular country.

title: 16 Products From Women Designers You Need to Know
author: @wired
content:
Slate Auto Fastback SUV

Tisha Johnson is a rarity in the car world: an automotive design leader who is not a man. Women are sometimes put in charge of the interiors or the materials, but few get to shape the whole look of a vehicle. As head of design at the EV-maker Slate, Johnson does. The pickup truck version of its EV starts at just under $25,000, making it the cheapest pickup on sale in the US, electric or not. Trouble is, cheap products are usually a compromise, and compromises rarely inspire affection. Johnson’s Slate, however, has won design awards, not just praise for its price tag.

“We didn’t want [Slate] to be a jerk,” Johnson says, “or look like a beast on the road.” That thinking shows in the truck itself—not just in its modular, add-on-friendly design (pictured here in its Fastback guise), but in the fact the EV was designed to be loved. Strong shoulders and approachable round headlamps were favored over macho arrowed surfacing. “The attraction that draws you to Slate is based on something that is lasting from inside out. It’s a deeper connection,” Johnson says. Some 180,000 reservations and counting for the Slate, along with those awards, seem to more than prove her point.

Away The Carry-On: Aluminum Edition

Away was founded in 2015 by entrepreneurs Jen Rubio and Steph Korey, both with backgrounds at the eyewear maker Warby Parker. In its first year, Away generated $12 million in sales and sold more than 100,000 stylish, reasonably priced suitcases. It has been an impressive rise, and the Softside Carry-on currently tops WIRED’s best buy list. Here however, we’ve chosen the aluminum version of the company’s handsome roll-aboard that’s built tough but perfectly sized for the overhead bin. It has a 32-liter capacity, dual TSA locks, 360-degree wheels, and an internal compression system. The signature hidden laundry bag remains a brilliant accoutrement.

Jelenew Mont Blanc Ultralight Long Windproof Jacket

Cofounded by six-time cycling world champion Marion Clignet, Jelenew combines female-specific articulated shaping, recycled nylon, mesh ventilation and an adjustable hem in a windproof shell that packs into a 6.3 x 9.8-inch bag. Clignet brought elite racing experience directly into the brand’s development, with the fit shaped around women’s proportions rather than scaled down from men’s clothing. This particular jacket uses 94 percent recycled nylon, a PFAS-free water-repellent treatment, UV protection, and mesh ventilation. Generous waist pockets and adjustable drawstrings add practical detail.

TaylorMade Kalea Gold Driver

Light, easy to launch, and forgiving, Kaela has been designed for women who want more performance than they can get from hacking a set of men’s clubs. Principal product-development engineer Michelle Penney helped lead the development of the range, with input from female TaylorMade employees, players, and and dedicated women’s advisory board. The final design takes into account the key differences in women’s swing profiles. The 460 cc carbon driver is 44 inches long, with 11.5- or 13.5-degree lofts and a lightweight 47-gram shaft intended to help generate speed without making the club harder to control.

Natural Cycles NC° Band

Cofounded by CERN physicist Elina Berglund Scherwitzl, who helped discover the Higgs boson, Natural Cycles makes the world’s first FDA-cleared birth-control app. Its screenless NC° Band syncs its health readings to the app. Wear it on your wrist while you sleep and it tracks your temperature, heart rate, and movement during the night, then automatically syncs all that data to your phone in the morning. Those numbers are fed into the app’s algorithm to give you accurate—Natural Cycles claims an impressive 93 percent accuracy—daily fertility guidance. A recently announced Whoop partnership helps strengthen both brand’s offerings too.

Adafruit Pimoroni Badgeware Badger

Ladyada, aka Limor Fried, became the first female engineer to appear on the cover of WIRED in April 2011, just six years after she founded Adafruit from her MIT dorm room. Her alias was inspired by 19th-century English mathematician and computing pioneer Ada Lovelace, which in turn provided inspiration for the brand’s name. Fried has grown Adafruit into a 100 percent woman-owned force in open-source electronics, making components, tools, and educational kits that lower the barrier to coding and hardware hacking. The company’s range spans beginner-friendly boards, wearable controllers, and touchscreens, alongside quirky maker gear such as the pictured programmable, wearable e-paper name badge.

Raide Women’s TrailTech Cargo Tank

More than just another running top, this multifunctional design combines an unpadded sports bra, a vest, and much of the carrying capacity of a small hydration pack in a single 4.6-ounce layer. Five well-positioned pockets hold up to 30 fluid ounces of water, a phone, your rain shell, and up to six fuel gels, all while keeping the load close to your body to help minimize bounce. Laser-perforated chest panels add ventilation, and the fit is designed around female anatomy rather than adapted from a men’s cut. It is a neat solution for runners who want to go the distance without adding layers on layers.

Vacheron Constantin Overseas Self-Winding

There was a time, not so long ago, when all serious timepieces had two clear traits. They were massive—we’re talking over 48 mm here, which fine if you have Schwarzenegger-sized forearms but useless for those who don’t—and they were aimed just at men. Women’s watches would have comparatively basic mechanical movements, or be quartz powered and covered in jewels.

Thankfully, general watch size trends have swung back the other way, and now small- and mid-size pieces are very much in demand. This means women with a serious eye for horology now have some truly excellent choices. This new Vacheron is a perfect example: Clocking in at 34.5 mm, this Overseas will suit both men and women very well in either stainless steel or pink gold. It’s a nearly exact shrunken version of the 41 mm model, and nothing has been dropped in the downsizing apart from the outer seconds track on the dial. The quick-release bracelet, two extra quick-change straps, 40-hour power reserve, and sapphire caseback are all present.

Dreame Miracle Pro

AI is drying hair now, or more specifically, adjusting temperature, heat, and airflow automatically. Dreame’s dryer also includes a conditioning essence atomizer and red light therapy to take extra care of your scalp. The 1,400-watt dryer monitors temperature 1,000 times per second to keep the airflow ultra consistent. The dryer also comes with four magnetic attachments: nozzles for styling, smoothing, and defrizzing, plus a diffuser. Snap one on, and the Miracle pro senses which one you’ve attached and adjusts the dryer’s power and heat for the best possible results.

Music Man St. Vincent HHH

Annie Clark, aka art-rocker St. Vincent, sketched the original shape for her signature guitar using angles that combine midcentury retro-futurism with the bold triangular tuxedo worn by avant-garde performer Klaus Nomi. She then worked through around 20 prototypes to get the weight, balance, and feel for the design just right. Despite the sharp lines, the body is heavily beveled with an exceptionally narrow waist, and Clark explicitly designed it to sit comfortably against a woman’s torso. Built from lightweight okoume wood, it weighs around 7.5 pounds, with a roasted maple neck that offers easy access to the upper frets (where the shredding happens). The three custom DiMarzio mini-humbuckers are controlled by a five-way selector.

KiwiCo STEM Kits

Chemical engineer and mother-of-three Sandra Oh Lin founded KiwiCo to make hands-on science, engineering and creative projects fun, practical, and easy to tackle at home. It offers kits for babies, kids, teens, and adults, with age-appropriate builds (and yes, we wouldn’t be surprised if the kids’ stuff was more advanced than the adults’) ranging from simple sensory play and mechanical grabbers to animatronics, marble roller coasters, and working desk lamps. Available individually or by subscription, everything that’s needed to build each device arrives in the box, with clear instructions and explanations of the ideas behind each project.

IDA Helia Pro

Informed by biometric data from professional women soccer players, IDA builds high-performance boots around women’s feet, combining specific fit with lightweight materials. Cofounder Laura Youngson started the company after seeing how poorly existing boots served women players. The Helia Pro packs in the tech with a lightweight mesh upper, a highly responsive soleplate made from Pebax thermoplastic, and a soft foam insole. There are also female-specific flex zones throughout the shoe, and shorter, rounded cleat studs laid out in a unique pattern that’s designed for firm ground and artificial grass.

New Balance Fresh Foam Cremorne Toe Safety Shoe

Looking closer to a pair of trail runners than conventional safety footwear, these are proof you don’t need to be clodhopping around in heavy boots to stay protected on the job site. The composite toe guards shield your piggies from impacts without the weight of steel, an anti-perforation layer protects the sole of your foot, and a reinforced heel support adds stability when you’re lifting loads. Its grippy outsole is designed for wet, slick, or oily floors, and offers antistatic protection while also being able to withstand temperatures of at least 572° Fahrenheit for 60 seconds. The shoes borrow foam cushioning and a springy polyurethane insert from New Balance’s athletic footwear to make long shifts easier on your feet.

Circular Smart Ring 3 Slim

We’re not quite at the point where smart rings are indistinguishable from jewelry, but the gap is closing. At just 1.9 grams, and with a noticeably slimmer profile than the second-generation model, Circular’s Ring 3 Slim blends in well, yet still tracks sleep, heart rate, blood oxygen level, skin temperature, daily activities, and heart-rate variability. It now adds NFC for contactless payments and practical vibration alerts and alarms. There’s also a larger Ring 3 Pro, which adds FDA-cleared electrocardiogram sensors for detecting signs of atrial fibrillation. Blood-pressure trends and glucose insights are planned for a later update.

Posedla Joyseat 3.0

Finally, a saddle that actually fits. Posedla sends an at-home imprint kit, then uses sit-bone measurements, riding position, and algorithmic modeling to 3D-print bespoke padding precisely profiled for your posterior. The resulting Joyseat is not merely made in a chosen width. Its shape and stiffness are individually generated too, using a custom TPU lattice rather than stock foam. Width can be specified from 130 to 170 mm in one millimeter increments, and Joyseat will also take into consideration the bike you use and what sorts of riding you do—whether you’re a racer, a weekend tourer, a bike camper, or a long-haul commuter.

Liv EnviLiv Advanced Pro 0-AXS

Bonnie Tu, chair of the company behind Giant bikes, founded Liv after struggling to find bikes that fitted properly. Liv designs from women’s biometric data, giving every frame size its own geometry, then applies its findings to a collection that includes city, gravel, commuter and elite bikes like the EnviLiv Advanced Pro. Its carbon frame, handlebars and stem are shaped using computer modelling and wind-tunnel testing to reduce drag, while 50 mm-deep carbon wheels and SRAM Force AXS wireless electronic gears complete the race-ready build. More importantly, fit is treated as a complete system, with stem length, handlebar width, crank length and saddle choice all selected to suit the rider rather than added later as generic components.

title: Why is This Octopus Hitching a Ride on a Dolphin? - Nautilus
content:
It’s a sight you don’t see often, or ever: a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) apparently hitching a ride on the back of a Risso’s dolphin (Grampus griseus) by clinging onto its fin.

Featured Video

The photo was taken off the coast of the U.K. by Bill Coulson from the citizen science initiative Risso’s Dolphin Project.

We don’t know what this unusual interaction means, but we do know that warming waters around this part of the southwest coast of England are leading to a bloom in octopuses. While Risso’s dolphins usually feed on squid, they’re quite partial to octopus as well, and so the interaction captured here is unlikely to be a friendly one (don’t expect a Pixar adaptation).

Dolphins usually spend their time in deeper waters further from the coast, but experts think the abundance of octopuses—a marine animal that lives much closer to the shore—might be tempting the Risso’s dolphins to new feeding grounds.

Read more: “Dolphins Eavesdrop on Their Prey—and Each Other”

“These photographs offer a fascinating glimpse into the feeding ecology of Risso’s dolphins and the changing marine environment around our coasts,” the University of Exeter’s Josh Symes said in a statement. “Risso’s dolphins are closely associated with cephalopods, and sightings like this help us understand how they’re responding to changing prey availability.”

Symes is part of a team investigating the octopus bloom—the biggest in 75 years—which not only provides extra food for dolphins, but also threatens the crabs, lobsters, and scallops that the cephalopods feed on. It’s believed that the creatures have moved from breeding grounds in the Channel Islands and northern France, encouraged by warming temperatures at higher latitudes.

Work is continuing to better understand how these shifts are impacting the marine ecosystem as a whole, and scientists need as many photographs and data points as possible to get a full picture. In fact, contributions to the project are often posted to its Instagram page. “The images also highlight the value of citizen science, as observations from volunteers are helping us build a clearer picture of marine wildlife across the southwest,” Symes said.

In other words, any evidence of dolphin or octopus activity is useful—whether they’re locked together in an unusual embrace or not.

title: On Not Being a Homeowner
author: Cheri Lucas Rowlands
content:
In this personal essay at The New Yorker, Anna Holmes writes about growing up in Davis, California, a college town near Sacramento; the financial challenges her mixed-race family faced; and what it means to come from a family without the generational wealth that can make homeownership, and the financial security that comes with it, possible.

It’s hard to hear people who own property grumble about how little money they have. One friend who regularly moans about money has a four-bedroom home on the West Coast and a vacation house in New England. I’m unmoved by the financial lamentations of another friend, who owns a town house in New York with an apartment for a nanny or an in-law. Stuff like this makes me want to scream. Demonstrate some modicum of self-awareness! Read the fucking room! When a friend told me that her parents were going to help her buy a second home, I made a pointed remark that it must be nice to have access to that sort of capital. She conceded the point, graciously, and we moved on.

title: Respecting our multi-branch lawmaking process
author: Chad Squitieri
content:
In my inaugural entry for this column, I critiqued the Supreme Court’s reliance on an abstract conception of the “separation of powers.” Because the Constitution does not contain a “separation of powers” clause, but instead contains a collection of specific provisions that enforce the separation of powers in specific ways, I contended that the court should more carefully refer to the specific constitutional provisions that support its decisions. In this second column entry, I would like to bring a similar level of specificity to the separation-of-powers provisions that address the federal lawmaking process. A close look at those provisions indicate that, if the court wishes to better respect the Constitution’s design, the court should abandon its practice of regularly treating Congress as if that branch can unilaterally make law.

Let’s start with some examples of the phenomenon in question. Judicial references to “Congress” simply making law are ubiquitous and have been offered by justices of different interpretive stripes. In 2025, Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote on behalf of a unanimous court that “Congress enacted ERISA to ‘protect . . . the interests of participants in employee benefit plans and their beneficiaries.’” That same year, Justice Amy Coney Barrett contended “that Congress did not intend for courts to consider” particular factors. More recently, Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in Learning Resources v. Trump that “[t]he Government points to no statute in which Congress used the word ‘regulate’ to authorize taxation.” In the same cases, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson added that “probing Congress’s intent is the right inquiry.” And in another high-profile example, Roberts contended in King v. Burwell that “Congress passed the Affordable Care Act to improve health insurance markets, not to destroy them.”

Many more examples could be offered. And to the extent those examples are only intended to suggest that Congress plays a role in making law, the examples are not particularly problematic. A problem does arise, however, when those routine references to congressional lawmaking allow a jurist to slip into thinking that Congress makes law alone. That is because, at least in the mine-run of cases, the Constitution does not empower Congress to unilaterally make law. Instead, the Constitution ordinarily requires Congress to make law in concert with the president. Thus, by routinely focusing on “Congress” as the relevant lawmaker, the court gives short shrift to the president’s role in the lawmaking process and risks systematically favoring one of the two political branches that the Constitution empowers to shape federal statutes.

At least three constitutional provisions speak to the president’s influence in the lawmaking process. The first is the presentment clause, which requires bills to be presented to the president for his potential veto. Because legislators in Congress know that they must present bills to the president, the presentment clause allows for the president’s legislative agenda to influence legislative text long before it is formally sent for presidential review. A legislator aiming to turn a bill into law, for example, would be wise to determine whether the bill is consistent with the president’s legislative agenda, as that can influence how the bill is drafted. A bill consistent with the president’s legislative agenda might be drafted to squeak by with simple majorities in the House and Senate (or a 60-vote majority in the Senate if the self-imposed filibuster is in play). A bill at odds with the president’s legislative agenda, by comparison, should be drafted in a way that can secure two-thirds support in each legislative chamber – which is the constitutionally required supermajority for overriding a presidential veto.

The second clause speaking to the president’s role in the lawmaking process is the recommendations clause, which states that the president “shall . . . recommend to [Congress’] Consideration such Measures as he shall judge necessary and expedient.” This can give the president an important first-mover advantage. Consider the State of the Union Address, where the president commonly makes legislative recommendations. After the president’s address, a large segment of the country typically rallies behind the president’s legislative proposals, while a separate segment of the country typically takes the opposing position. What those competing segments share is a focus on the president’s legislative proposals, giving the president’s proposals vastly more attention than what might be offered to proposals from ordinary legislators.

The third clause is the vice president as presiding officer clause, which empowers the vice president to cast tie-breaking votes in the Senate. While the recommendation and presentment clauses grant the president the ability to influence legislation toward the start and end of the lawmaking process, the vice president affords the president opportunities to influence legislation during the middle of the lawmaking process. As the Supreme Court recognized in Trump v. United States, “the President may frequently rely on the Vice President in his capacity as President of the Senate to advance the President’s agenda in Congress.”

To be sure, although the president has tremendous influence in the lawmaking process, it does not follow that the president will always get his way in that process. Congress might ignore a presidential recommendation, override a presidential veto, or make political alliances so that the vice president is not given the chance to cast tie-breaking votes. But even in those situations, the president’s mere participation in the process can influence what ultimately becomes law. As an example, and to refer again to the dynamics imposed by the presentment clause, legislators who expect a presidential veto might account for it by initially drafting legislative text so that it can secure the necessary two-thirds veto-override support in Congress. Thus, a bill that might have been written one way had the president not been involved in the lawmaking process might be written very differently simply because of the president’s role.

In short, the president plays an important part in the lawmaking process. Given as much, the Supreme Court should abandon its practice of regularly referring to “Congress” as if that branch makes law alone. Rather, the court should more routinely refer to both branches involved in the multi-branch lawmaking process. The court can do so by referring to statutes “passed by Congress and signed by the President,” or to national policy “made by Congress and the President in the legislative process,” to borrow two helpful phrases used by Justice Brett Kavanaugh.

My call for the court to stop treating Congress as a unilateral lawmaker is not simply a matter of semantics. Substantial interpretive consequences flow from recognizing the president’s role in the lawmaking process. I will conclude by briefly discussing three such consequences here (you can find additional analysis of two of these points in a forthcoming Alabama Law Review article).

First, recognizing the president’s role in the lawmaking process gives reason to question methods of statutory interpretation that focus on legislative intent and rely on legislative history, which justices such as Jackson have strongly advocated for. To the extent that a jurist’s focus on “legislative intent” means a focus on “congressional intent,” that focus is in serious tension with the multi-branch lawmaking process outlined in the Constitution. That is because, even if one assumes that the 535 legislators in Congress share an identifiable intent, that congressional intent might be at odds with the president’s intent. An exclusive focus on Congress’ intent is therefore constitutionally problematic. At minimum, any judicial focus on “legislative intent” should be broad enough to include the collective lawmaking intent of both Congress and the president.

Relatedly, a jurist who uses legislative history to elucidate legislative intent should be careful to consider legislative history from both Congress (e.g., committee reports and floor speeches) and the president (e.g., signing statements and presidential speeches). Otherwise, the jurist would risk systematically favoring the lawmaking views of one of the two branches that the Constitution empowers to collectively shape federal law.

Second, and unintuitively, recognizing the president’s role in the lawmaking process could help the court empower Congress. The court has recently signaled an interest in empowering Congress by overruling Chevron deference and embracing the major questions doctrine – two doctrinal moves that reduce the executive branch’s ability to sidestep Congress by unilaterally enacting regulatory policies. But the court is not likely to catch each and every executive-branch effort to sidestep Congress. And so the court might complement its recent doctrinal moves by giving presidents the incentive to more frequently turn to Congress as a partner in the multi-branch lawmaking process.

The court can give presidents incentives to turn to Congress by signaling that statutes will not be systematically interpreted in favor of Congress’s “intent,” but will instead be interpreted neutrally and in a way that can sometimes benefit the president. The situation might be analogized to a businessperson who has a new incentive to come to a contract-negotiation table, rather than pursue unilateral action, after learning that the contract will be interpreted neutrally and in favor of neither contracting party.

To be sure, jurists who worry that modern presidents already exercise too much power might object to interpreting the end-product of the multi-branch lawmaking process (i.e., legislative text) in a way that does not favor Congress over the president. Those jurists might instead think that the best way to respond to an overly powerful president is to empower Congress by treating Congress as if it unilaterally makes law. But that would be giving Congress more power than the Constitution affords. And the proper solution to any one branch exercising too much power is not to double the error by granting too much power to a separate branch. Instead, the proper solution is to ensure that no branch oversteps constitutional limits. And enforcing constitutional limits brings us to a third and final consequence that follows from recognizing the president’s role in the lawmaking process: a need to reconceptualize the nondelegation doctrine.

The nondelegation doctrine imposes a constitutional limit on statutory delegations of lawmaking discretion to the executive branch. The doctrine is not aggressively enforced, and it has been something of a dead letter in recent decades. Jurists who are concerned that modern presidents exercise too much authority, such as Justice Neil Gorsuch, have therefore looked to reinvigorating the nondelegation doctrine as a means of reining in the executive branch. It should come as a relief to those jurists, then, to note that respecting the president’s role in the lawmaking process would not give independent reason to abandon efforts to reinvigorate the nondelegation doctrine. However, respecting the president’s role in the lawmaking process would require the nondelegation doctrine to be reconceptualized so that it better accounts for the constitution’s design.

Today, the nondelegation doctrine is sometimes conceptualized as a limit on Congress’ ability to delegate Congress’ lawmaking power to the president. But that is a problematic framing because the Constitution does not grant Congress unilateral lawmaking power in the first place (bracketing potential complications relating to special topics such as federal property). Yes, Congress alone is vested with certain “legislative Powers,” but, as I have explained, to use those powers to make law, Congress must ordinarily work through a multi-branch lawmaking process that includes the president. Thus, a better conception of the nondelegation doctrine would be to understand it as limiting Congress and the president from agreeing to statutes that empower anyone else besides Congress and the president (acting in concert through the proper channels) from making law. That would mean limiting Congress’s and the president’s ability to statutorily empower the president to make law unilaterally.

***

The court frequently treats Congress as if that branch makes law alone. But the Constitution sets out an arduous multi-branch lawmaking process that allows for the president to shape legislative text from top to bottom. Going forward, the court should better account for the Constitution’s multi-branch lawmaking process by more regularly referencing both the Congress and the president when referring to the creation of federal statutes. Doing so would help the court better respect the important interpretive consequences that flow from recognizing the president’s role in shaping federal law.
